documents.title: Some Moral and Technical Consequences of Automation—A Refutation

records.statement: Wiener's Cybernetics (1948, read in the 2019 reissue) states that the modern industrial revolution is bound to devalue the human brain, at least in its simpler and more routine decisions, and that, taking that revolution as accomplished, the average human being of mediocre attainments or less has nothing to sell that it is worth anyone's money to buy.

attested.note: Read in the MIT Press reissue of the 1961 second edition; the 1948 and 1961 printings were not compared.

records.tier: tier 2 (a mathematician's book, not an economist's scholarly work or a core economics venue), by the economics collection's rule of 2026-10-11
records.earliestLocatedFlag: On its 1948 date it would precede M06a's tier-1 earliest located text (Buckingham, 1955-10-14), but it is tier 2 and its wording is attested only from 2019 here. Whether it becomes M06a's earliest located tier-2 text depends on retrieving the 1948 printing; flagged, not assigned.
records.qualification: A statement about the effect of automation of routine decisions on the market value of ordinary labour, made in the book's introduction. The book adds that 'the answer' is a society based on human values other than buying or selling.

evidence.passage: The modern industrial revolution is similarly bound to devalue the human brain, at least in its simpler and more routine decisions.
the average human being of mediocre attainments or less has nothing to sell that it is worth anyone’s money to buy.

maintainerDecision.effect: Admitted with the attested date (2019) and no headline change; a library is asked for the 1948 printing.

records.statement: Wiener's Cybernetics (1948, read in the 2019 reissue) states that those who have contributed to the new science do not have the choice of suppressing its technical developments, and that the most “any of us” can do by suppression is to put the subject into the hands of its most irresponsible and most venal engineers.
records.missing: Competition between developers or states: the passage says suppression by the scientists concerned would hand the subject to others, without naming rival developers or states.
records.qualification: The developments in question are those of cybernetics and automatic machines, which the book says have 'great possibilities for good and for evil'. Recorded as context after the same-family audit (F2); a cross-family check may read C3 more broadly, in which case it would be an articulation dated 1948 but attested 2019.

evidence.passage: We do not even have the choice of suppressing these new technical developments. They belong to the age, and the most any of us can do by suppression is to put the development of the subject into the hands of the most irresponsible
evidence.note: The sentence continues 'and most venal of our engineers'.

maintainerDecision.effect: Admitted with the attested date (2019) and no headline change; a library is asked for the 1948 printing.

records.statement: Wiener's Cybernetics (1948, read in the 2019 reissue) says that the new development makes the metaphorical dominance of the machines, as imagined by Samuel Butler, a most immediate and non-metaphorical problem.
records.missing: Succession as the leading intelligence: the next sentences describe the problem as machines doing human labour as 'mechanical slaves', not as machines replacing people as the dominant intelligence.
records.qualification: The passage also names Butler (see the link record).

evidence.passage: it makes the metaphorical dominance of the machines, as imagined by Samuel Butler, a most immediate and non-metaphorical problem.
evidence.note: A page break (running head 'Introduction', p. 40) falls after 'Samuel'. Matched with the page break's running head and download stamp skipped.
evidence.matchText: it makes the metaphorical dominance of the machines, as imagined by Samuel […] Butler, a most immediate and non-metaphorical problem.

records.statement: The supplementary chapter IX of Wiener's Cybernetics (second edition, 1961) states that the checker-playing machine described by Samuel and Watanabe can learn to defeat the man that programmed it in a fairly consistent way.

engagement.rationale: States a machine result that goes beyond its programmer's own play, without arguing here against the premise in general terms.

records.qualification: A report of Samuel's and Watanabe's results, cited to Samuel (1959) and Watanabe (1960). That a machine plays better than its programmer is contrary to a strong reading of U01 (no capability beyond its maker's); the chapter does not claim that the machine's output goes beyond its instructions and their consequences. Wording read in the 2019 reissue only; not compared with a 1961 printing.

evidence.locator: Chapter IX, 'On Learning and Self-Reproducing Machines'
evidence.passage: can learn to defeat the man that programmed it in a fairly consistent way on the basis of from 10 to 20 operating hours of programming.
evidence.note: The subject is 'The checker-playing machine described by Samuel and Watanabe'.

crossFamily.result: corrected: the inferential distinction is stated in the qualification.

maintainerDecision.effect: Admitted with the attested date (2019) and no headline change; a library is asked for the 1948 printing.

records.statement: Wiener's article in Science (6 May 1960) says that the assumption that machines cannot possess any degree of originality, often stated as 'nothing can come out of the machine which has not been put into it', should be rejected in its entirety, and states his thesis that machines can and do transcend some of the limitations of their designers.

engagement.rationale: Argues from game-playing machines that learn, and from machines acting faster than their operators can follow, that a machine's performance can outrun what its designers comprehend.

records.qualification: Wiener contests the assumption in order to argue that machines may be “both effective and dangerous”; that argument is recorded on B6 in the dataset. Samuel's reply of September 1960 states the contrary.

evidence.locator: p. 1355, left column, paragraph beginning 'Before commencing'
evidence.passage: This is the assumption that machines cannot possess any degree of originality. This frequently takes the form of a statement that nothing can come out of the machine which has not been put into it.
evidence.note: The preceding sentence says the attitude 'should be rejected in its entirety'.

evidence.passage: It is my thesis that machines can and do transcend some of the limitations of their designers, and that in doing so they may be both effective and dangerous.

records.statement: Samuel's 'Some Studies in Machine Learning Using the Game of Checkers' (IBM Journal, July 1959) states in its abstract that enough work has been done to verify that a computer can be programmed so that it will learn to play a better game of checkers than can be played by the person who wrote the program.

time.note: As on the dataset's records of the article.

engagement.rationale: Reports a result contrary to the claim that a machine can do no more than its programmer specifies, without discussing the claim.

records.qualification: The article does not mention Lovelace or the objection; that its result is contrary to U01 is the pack's reading, not a claim the article makes: a program that learns to beat its author still follows the learning rules it was given. Read in an undated later reprint that attributes the article to July 1959, whose wording was not compared with the 1959 printing. Samuel's reply to Wiener (1960) states U01 in its indexed abstract; the two are recorded separately.

evidence.passage: Enough work has been done to verify the fact that a computer can be programmed so that it will learn to play a better game of checkers than can be played by the person who wrote the program.
evidence.matchText: Enough work has been done to verify the fact that a computer can be programmed so that it will learn to playa better game of checkers than can be played by the person who wrote the program.
evidence.note: The text layer reads 'playa'; the page image reads 'play a'.

crossFamily.result: corrected: undated reprint stated; the contrary reading kept as an interpretation.

records.statement: The indexed abstract of Samuel's reply to Wiener (Science, 16 September 1960) states that the machine does not possess a will and that its so-called conclusions are only the logical consequences of its input.
records.qualification: Rests on the indexed abstract only; the article was not read. The abstract is the PubMed record's text and may be the journal's summary rather than Samuel's own words. The article body should be read before admission (Codex list). The author of the abstract is not known, so its role as primary evidence is uncertain (audit F12). Not to be admitted before the article is read.

evidence.locator: NCBI efetch XML, Article/Abstract/AbstractText, second sentence
evidence.passage: The abstract says the machine has no will and that its so-called "conclusions" are only the logical consequences of its input, revealed by the mechanistic functioning of an inanimate assemblage of parts.
evidence.note: Paraphrased because the source is under 50 words and the sentence exceeds 25 words.

crossFamily.result: not checkable: article body unavailable (403); paraphrase matches the indexed abstract; the hold on admission stands.

maintainerDecision.effect: Held until the article itself is read; not admitted.
